notes: AG reference on unduly lenient child pornography sentence; dismissal and Oliver guidelines are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: AG reference: unduly lenient sentence for paedophile bulletin board administrator
key_facts: Earl Webster Cox pleaded guilty to conspiring to distribute indecent photographs of children as administrator of the Ranchi paedophile bulletin board and to making level 1 and 2 indecent images.
The Crown accepted a basis of plea that Cox facilitated distribution of website addresses without knowing image levels and without uploading images himself.
The Recorder imposed 12 months' imprisonment on the conspiracy count with concurrent short terms on specimen possession counts.
The Solicitor General referred the conspiracy sentence as unduly lenient, arguing the bulletin board content showed knowledge of hardcore material.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference for leave to refer and review of an unduly lenient Crown Court sentence for child pornography offences.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to refer granted but the reference dismissed; the 12-month sentence on count 1 was not unduly lenient.
enrichment.ratio: On an unduly lenient reference the court cannot sentence on a factual basis rejected by responsible prosecuting counsel in the Crown Court; where the prosecution conceded ignorance of content levels, a 12-month sentence for facilitating distribution at an assumed level above 2, after guilty plea and mitigation, was not unduly lenient under the Oliver guidelines.
legal_issues: Whether the sentencing judge could infer knowledge of high-level child pornography from bulletin board postings
Whether the Solicitor General could rely on fresh evidence on a reference
Appropriate sentence for an administrator facilitating distribution without uploading images
Whether anal/vaginal intercourse between children falls within Oliver level 2
linked_authorities: R v Oliver and others [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 15

notes: Construction payment and arbitration stay appeal; Halki and section 111 analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Collins v Baltic Quay: stay of payment claim under JCT arbitration clause

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Collins Contractors carried out minor works at Baltic Quay under a JCT Minor Works contract with an adjudication and arbitration clause.
The employer paid four progress certificates but withheld payment certified in certificate No 5; the contractor determined the contract for non-payment and sued for about £53,777.
The contractor argued section 111 meant no effective withholding notice barred payment and entitled it to judgment.
The employer applied under section 9(4) for a stay because a dispute existed within the arbitration agreement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Technology and Construction Court order staying proceedings under section 9 of the Arbitration Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the employer was entitled to a stay of the whole action, including the certificate and final account claims.
enrichment.ratio: Section 111 of the Housing Grants Act governs substantive payment rights but is silent on whether such claims must be litigated or arbitrated; under section 9(4) and The Halki a stay must be granted whenever a dispute falls within a valid arbitration clause, regardless of whether the defendant has an arguable defence on the merits.
legal_issues: Whether failure to serve a section 111 withholding notice prevents a stay under section 9
Meaning of 'dispute' for arbitration and adjudication in construction contracts
Whether certificate-based payment claims are indisputable like bills of exchange
Application of The Halki to post-1996 Arbitration Act stays

Rupert Morgan Building Services (LLC) v Jervis [2004] 1 WLR 1867

notes: Police defamation and qualified privilege appeal; Thorpe principles and late slander amendment fully covered.

enrichment.short_title: Wood v West Midlands Police: qualified privilege for pre-trial police letters to insurers
key_facts: DCI Mulligan wrote to insurance industry contacts warning them that Gary Hart, who worked at Vehicle Salvage Group, was using the business as a front for vehicle ringing after Hart's arrest.
Ben Wood, VSG's public face though not named in the letters, sued the Chief Constable for libel by republication and later slander from a related telephone call.
The trial judge struck out qualified privilege on summary judgment, applying R v Chief Constable of North Wales Police ex parte Thorpe.
A jury awarded £45,000 after a late amendment added a slander claim based on Mulligan's call to Neil Simpson.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with limited permission on qualified privilege, late amendment to plead slander, and contingent challenge to damages.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; qualified privilege defence rightly rejected and the late slander amendment was a tenable exercise of discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Police disclosure of damaging information about unconvicted suspects to insurers is not protected by qualified privilege unless justified by a specific public duty after careful assessment; pre-conviction letters anticipating guilt and commercially harming innocent associates fail Thorpe and cannot sustain privilege, and a slander claim arising from the same facts may be allowed after limitation under section 32A where rule 17.4(2) is satisfied.
legal_issues: Whether police letters to insurers about a bailed suspect were on an occasion of qualified privilege
Application of Thorpe public law disclosure principles to defamation
Permissibility of a very late amendment to plead slander after limitation expired
Whether Kearns requires a pre-existing publisher-recipient relationship
linked_authorities: R v Chief Constable of North Wales Police, ex parte Thorpe [1999] QB 396
Kearns v General Council of the Bar [2003] EWCA Civ 331
Halford v Chief Constable of Hampshire [2003] EWCA Civ 102

notes: Kenyan asylum appeals; Subesh/IAT role and restoration of adjudicators' decisions are authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: P and M v SSHD: IAT error on Kenyan asylum claims for domestic violence and FGM
key_facts: P, a Kenyan woman, fled prolonged domestic violence by her police-connected husband; an adjudicator granted asylum and Article 3/8 relief finding discriminatory lack of state protection for women.
M, a younger Kenyan woman, feared forced genital mutilation by her Mungiki sect father after her mother and sister were mutilated; an adjudicator also allowed her appeal.
The IAT reversed both decisions, re-weighing facts without oral evidence and raising internal relocation for P for the first time on appeal.
The Secretary of State conceded social group and sufficiency-of-protection errors but sought remittal rather than restoration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals to the Court of Appeal from IAT decisions reversing adjudicators' asylum and human rights determinations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; the adjudicators' asylum decisions restored for both P and M, with Article 8 for P left open.
enrichment.ratio: The IAT is an appellate body bound by Subesh finality principles and must not rehear fact-sensitive asylum findings de novo without error; where adjudicators correctly applied Shah and Islam and the IAT's intervention was flawed, the court should restore the first-instance decision rather than remit when nothing was wrong with the adjudicator's determination.
legal_issues: Proper IAT approach to fact findings under Subesh
Whether Kenyan women constitute a particular social group for Refugee Convention purposes
Domestic violence plus discriminatory lack of state protection as persecution
Whether internal relocation could be raised for the first time on IAT appeal
linked_authorities: Subesh v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 56
R v Immigration Appeal Tribunal, ex parte Shah and Islam [1999] 2 AC 629
Oleed v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] EWCA Civ 1906

notes: Shoplifting sentencing guidance with three applications; principles and individual outcomes are clear.

enrichment.short_title: R v Page and Maher: Court of Appeal guidance on shoplifting sentences
key_facts: The Court heard three shoplifting-related sentencing appeals together to give current guidance on isolated adult shoplifters.

Page, a habitual shoplifter with old burglary convictions, received 3 years 10 months total including 3½ years for a serious dwelling burglary and consecutive terms for restaurant deception and theft.
Maher, a persistent shoplifter with foil-lined bags and drug addiction, received 2 years 3 months after revocation of a DTTO for multiple thefts and going equipped.
Stewart received 3 years for a dwelling burglary using a child to gain entry plus shoplifting, and was refused leave to appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for leave to appeal against sentence referred direct to the Court of Appeal Criminal Division.
enrichment.outcome: Guidance given; Page's burglary sentence reduced to 2½ years (total 2 years 10 months); Maher's total reduced to 12 months; Stewart's application refused.
enrichment.ratio: Custody should be a sentence of last resort for first-time adult shoplifters; short terms up to 1-2 months may suit persistent minor shoplifting, and even extensive persistent offending on plea will rarely require more than 12-18 months and should not exceed 2 years unless organised gang offending or violence is involved.
legal_issues: Appropriate custodial levels for habitual shoplifters
Totality where burglary and shoplifting are sentenced together
Whether older shoplifting authorities remain good law
Treatment of drug-driven shoplifting and DTTO breaches

Attorney-General's Reference No 64 of 2003 [2004] 2 Cr App R(S) 106

notes: Educational negligence for Asperger's misplacement; liability upheld but causation narrowed on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: DN v Greenwich: educational psychologist negligence and Asperger's placement
key_facts: DN, later diagnosed with Asperger's Syndrome, was placed in Moatbridge EBD school after a 1990 educational psychology report by Mr Moreland.
The trial judge found Moreland negligent for failing to identify communication needs, omitting psychometric tests, and not recommending a specialist school.
Psychiatric experts agreed Moatbridge was inappropriate and continuous appropriate education would likely have improved outcomes, but disagreed on how much.
DN later developed severe behavioural problems, fire-setting, arson convictions, and a restriction order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a split trial finding liability and causation for negligence by a local authority educational psychologist, with damages to be reassessed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on liability; causation remitted with direction that damages must reflect balance-of-probabilities loss, not lost opportunity, and exclude arson consequences under Clunis.
enrichment.ratio: An educational psychologist owes a duty to assess complex communication needs with reasonable skill; misplacement in an EBD school can be negligent even without an Asperger's diagnosis, but causation for psychiatric and earning-capacity loss requires proof on the balance of probabilities that a better education would probably have prevented entrenched behavioural harm, not merely improved chances.
legal_issues: Standard of care of an LEA educational psychologist in 1990
Admissibility of a defendant professional's opinion evidence without independent expert
Causation of psychiatric injury and fire-setting from wrong school placement
Recoverability of damages for criminal conduct consequences
linked_authorities: Phelps v Hillingdon London Borough Council [2001] 2 AC 619
Clunis v Camden and Islington Health Authority [1998] QB 978
Hotson v East Berkshire Area Health Authority [1987] AC 750

notes: Police injury pension JR applying Stunt; quashing and remittal are clearly ordered.

enrichment.short_title: Merseyside Police v Gidlow: injury award for stress from grievance procedure
key_facts: Sergeant Reilly-Cooper developed mixed anxiety/depression after a civilian employee's grievance and unsubstantiated 1996 touching allegation were handled without full investigation.
He was medically retired in 2002 and sought an injury pension on the basis the psychiatric condition was an injury received in execution of duty.
Dr Jones certified the disablement was not duty-related; on appeal Dr Gidlow upheld the claim, finding management handling of the grievance caused the injury.
Merseyside Police Authority challenged the referee's decision by judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a medical referee's certificate under regulation H2 of the Police Pensions Regulations 1987.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; Dr Gidlow's decision quashed and the appeal remitted to a different medical referee.
enrichment.ratio: Psychiatric injury arising from a police officer's reaction to a workplace grievance and perceived failure of management to vindicate him against an allegation is not an injury received in the execution of duty within regulation A11; it results from being a police officer subject to employment processes, following Stunt, and cannot be equated with injury while on duty.
legal_issues: Construction of 'injury received in the execution of duty' for psychiatric disablement
Distinction between Kellam work-stress cases and Stunt disciplinary/grievance stress
Whether grievance procedures differ from disciplinary proceedings for injury award purposes
Limits of a medical referee's role in assessing legal causation
linked_authorities: R (Stunt) v Mallett [2001] EWCA Civ 265
R (South Wales Police Authority) v Kellam [2000] ICR 632

notes: Section 41 cross-examination and inconsistent verdicts appeal; both grounds rejected.

enrichment.short_title: R v TW: section 41 and inconsistent verdicts in familial sex offences trial

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: TW, aged 71, was convicted by a 10-2 majority of raping and indecently assaulting his blind sister-in-law who lived in his home.
The defence case was consent to the convicted acts and denial of the acquitted acts; another sister was said to have influenced false allegations.
Defence counsel sought to cross-examine the complainant on past comments about male friends at a club to support honest belief in consent.
The judge refused cross-examination beyond non-sexual 'friendships', finding section 41 engaged and the questioning irrelevant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge on section 41 cross-examination and inconsistent verdicts grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the section 41 ruling was correct and the convictions were not logically inconsistent with acquittals on denied acts.
enrichment.ratio: Cross-examination about a complainant's past statements regarding previous sexual behaviour falls within section 41 unless the defence unequivocally challenges prior false allegations with an evidential basis; where consent is the primary issue and the past behaviour is remote, refusal of leave is a proper exercise of discretion, and acquittal on counts the defendant denied while conviction on admitted acts with disputed consent is not inconsistent.
legal_issues: Whether proposed cross-examination on past statements fell within section 41
Proper exercise of discretion to grant section 41 leave for belief in consent
Whether convictions and acquittals on the same complainant's evidence were inconsistent
Application of R v T and H and R v C and B
linked_authorities: R v T and H [2001] EWCA Crim 1877
R v C and B [2003] EWCA Crim 29

notes: Interlocutory patent case management; stay, section 1782 and amendment rulings are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Nokia v InterDigital: GSM patent revocation, stay and US section 1782 discovery
key_facts: Nokia sought revocation of three UK patents relating to wireless loop TDM technology that InterDigital claimed were essential to GSM standards.
InterDigital applied to stay the revocation action pending a related ICC arbitration on royalty payability under a 1999 licence.
Nokia also pursued US section 1782 discovery from Ericsson concerning prior art and the Ericsson settlement licence.
InterDigital sought to restrain the section 1782 application and strike out Nokia's standard-essentiality pleading.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case management conference in the Patents Court on stay, section 1782 injunction, and pleading amendment applications.
enrichment.outcome: Stay refused; section 1782 injunction and declaratory relief refused; Nokia permitted to amend to seek non-essentiality declarations for patents asserted essential to GSM.
enrichment.ratio: A properly constituted patent revocation action should proceed to trial where validity was excluded from arbitration and no ADR agreement can revoke patents; a party may use US section 1782 to obtain third-party evidence unless the request is abusive, and essentiality to an ETSI standard may support a declaration of non-infringement/non-essentiality where the patentee asserts GSM essentiality.
legal_issues: Whether revocation proceedings should be stayed pending ICC arbitration
When the English court may restrain a section 1782 discovery application
Admissibility and relevance of Ericsson litigation documents to revocation
Whether declarations as to GSM standard essentiality are permissible

notes: Iraq war protest coach case; preventive action upheld but return detention unlawful.

enrichment.short_title: Laporte v Gloucestershire Police: turning back Iraq protest coaches

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Protesters including Laporte travelled by coach to demonstrate at RAF Fairford against the Iraq war on 22 March 2003.
Police intelligence indicated Wombles activists on board with items to disrupt the protest and gain entry to the base.
Coaches were stopped near Lechlade, searched under section 60, and prevented from proceeding; passengers were escorted back to London.
Passengers were confined on coaches for about two and a half hours unable to leave even to use toilet facilities.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from judicial review declarations on lawfulness of police action at a lay-by and during the return journey.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed and cross-appeal dismissed; preventing coaches reaching Fairford was lawful but forcibly returning and detaining passengers on the journey to London was unlawful.
enrichment.ratio: Police may take reasonable preventive action short of arrest where a senior officer honestly and reasonably apprehends a real and proximate risk of breach of the peace, including collectively preventing coach passengers from reaching the site when individual identification is impracticable, but confining protesters on a two-and-a-half hour return journey without arrest goes beyond proportionate breach-of-the-peace prevention.
legal_issues: Imminence required for preventive action versus arrest for breach of the peace
Whether blanket action against all coach passengers was lawful
Compatibility with Articles 5, 10 and 11 ECHR
Distinction between preventing travel to a protest and detaining protesters en route home
linked_authorities: Moss v McLachlan [1985] IRLR 76
Albert v Lavin [1982] AC 546
Duncan v Jones [1936] 1 KB 218
